💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when discussing movies from the ‘90s, there are some films that get mentioned all the time.
  • I'd also be remiss if I didn’t bring up films that came out during the Disney Renaissance, such as The Lion King and Aladdin.
  • However, do you want to know what movie ISN’T on our list?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when discussing movies from the ‘90s, there are some films that get mentioned all the time. I'm talking about movies like Pulp Fiction, The Silence of the Lambs, and, of course, The Shawshank Redemption (Even though I think it's just “good” and not great).

I'd also be remiss if I didn’t bring up films that came out during the Disney Renaissance, such as The Lion King and Aladdin. Why am I bringing up those movies? You already know them and have probably already seen them. In fact, you can find many of the most beloved films from the ‘90s on our list of the 100 best films from that decade.

However, do you want to know what movie ISN’T on our list? The 1995 masterpiece (Yes, masterpiece) 12 Monkeys. I actually think it’s one of the best films from that decade, and here’s why.

A lot of people like to bring up great opening scenes in films, but do you know what I don’t think gets enough credit? Great opening songs, and look, I get it. Many older, typically black-and-white films (or westerns!) began with opening credits and stirring music before we met the characters. But nowadays, most films jump right into the action (in medias res, as it were).

Sources indicate that however, 12 Monkeys probably has my favorite intro from the ‘90s, and it’s entirely because of that accordion-driven song, “Suite Punta del Este” by the Argentine composer, Astor Pantaleón Piazzolla. This is after we get a green text scrawl telling us that 5 billion people will die from a deadly virus, and that the survivors will move underground. Oh, and these are the words from a diagnosed paranoid schizophrenic.

This text is then followed up by the aforementioned, driving accordion song, and then a close-up of a child’s eyes as the kid watches somebody get gunned down in an airport. Absolute cinema!

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, I love a good time travel story, and 12 Monkeys has one of my favorites of any film. The story concerns a convict named Cole (Bruce Willis) who is sent back in time to investigate what caused the virus that killed 99% of the human population. He’s tasked with learning who the “Army of the 12 Monkeys” are, since they’re suspected of releasing the virus, as there are records of them writing, “We did it!”.

Sources indicate that sounds simple enough. But the problem is, Cole’s time traveling gets overshot, and he ends up in 1990 rather than 1996. Because he sounds crazy - talking about the end of the world and whatnot - he gets committed to a mental institution. It’s here that he meets another patient, played by Brad Pitt, but is then yanked back into the future, only to be sent to World War 1.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot more wonky time travel shenanigans, but we learn what the message of “We did it!” meant (and it has nothing to do with the virus). We also learn that the child from the beginning who witnessed the shooting is actually Cole witnessing himself as an adult getting shot! Trippy!

Lastly, Brad Pitt is just so good in this movie. He plays a mental asylum patient, and the closest thing I can compare his performance to is Johnny Depp wigging out in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.

Recent findings suggest that pitt’s character, Jeffrey Goines, looks both extremely tired and also hopped up on goofballs at the same time. He’s erratic, unpredictable, and simultaneously both funny and scary. It’s little wonder why he was nominated for Best Supporting Actor for this performance.

In a recent development, in every way, the acting, the storytelling, the music, the everything! just makes 12 Monkeys one of the best movies of the ‘90s, and an absolute gem that more people need to talk about.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's the most famous film in history? "Star Wars"? "Citizen Kane"? "Casablanca"? Victor Fleming's "The Wizard of Oz" has to be in contention. "Oz" remains as beloved almost a century after its premiere as it was in its day, and everything of note about the movie is embedded into pop culture, from the Yellow Brick Road to the characters who walk it to the Flying Monkeys. Ever since the 1950s, the film has become a staple of television programming, ensuring generations that came long after the movie itself still learn from an early age to cherish it.

According to recent reports, margaret Hamilton as The Wicked Witch of the West is the definitive cultural image of a wicked witch. Her green skin, black outfit with a pointed hat, and, of course, her broom are the blueprint for countless other witches (not to mention, Halloween costumes).

In a recent development, "Oz" wasn't the first ever color film, despite misconceptions otherwise, but it still represents a turning point. One reason the error sticks is how well it maps onto the movie's narrative. Dorothy Gale's (Judy Garland) story begins in plain old Kansas, shot in black and white. Then, when she lands in Oz, the movie turns into technicolor. Even today, the film's rainbow-colored fantasy remains a beautiful spectacle.

Industry observers note that many, many unofficial "Wizard of Oz" sequels and prequels have been made, including various animated movies and TV series. Later "Oz" movies range from the (surprisingly frightening) 1985 sequel "Return to Oz" to Sam Raimi's 2013 prequel about the wizard, "Oz the Great and Powerful." Then of course, there's the stage musical (and now two-part movie) "Wicked," the only "Oz"-inspired work that even comes close to the original movie's cultural status.

Sources indicate that as you almost certainly know, during "The Wizard of Oz," Dorothy and her little dog Toto get swept away by  a twister to the Land of Oz. After a grand adventure, she realizes the power to go home was with her all along in the ruby slippers gifted to her by Glinda the Good Witch (Billie Burke). So, calling on the slippers' power, Dorothy closes her eyes and wakes up in her bed back in Kansas after affirming "There's no place like home!" (suggesting, unlike in its source material, Dorothy's adventure was all a dream). She then declares to her Aunt Em (Clara Blandick) and everyone else present that there is, indeed, no place like home.

At the beginning of "The Wizard of Oz," Dorothy wants to see more of the world beyond Kansas, as she sings in "Somewhere Over The Rainbow." She finally runs away to save her dog Toto from the cruel Mrs. Gulch (Margaret Hamilton), but then rushes back when traveling performer Professor Marvel (Frank Morgan) warns her that her aunt, uncle, and friends back at the farm worry for her.

Recent findings suggest that in a film and TV landscape where it feels like every other video game is getting an adaptation, we can add another (unexpected) candidate to the pile. Variety just broke that the ‘90s shoot-‘em-up series Metal Slug is getting a live-action movie. As you might expect, given that Metal Slug publisher SNK is owned by the Saudi Arabian government's Electronic Gaming Development Company (EGDC), the film is being made by the Saudi-backed production studio The Arena.

The proposed movie will follow the characters Marco Rossi, Tarma Roving, Eri Kasamoto, and Fio Germi, who Variety describes as “four misfits and inseparable friends who become the army’s most unlikely squad — until General Morden’s tyrannical uprising forces them to become the improbable heroes standing between the world and an even greater evil lurking behind him.” The inclusion of these characters is unsurprising: Marco and Tarma are the protagonists of the original Metal Slug, while Eri and Fio first appeared in Metal Slug 2. The most recent game in the series was Metal Slug Tactics, a turn-based roguelike RPG that marked a big departure from Metal Slug’s typical run-and-gun gameplay. Another more traditional reboot is in the works.

It has been revealed that the movie is being written by James Morosini, an actor and filmmaker who previously wrote, directed, and starred in the 2022 comedy I Love My Dad. Melissa Goodall and Sajan Algiri from The Arena are overseeing the adaptation.

It has been revealed that beyond Metal Slug, The Arena is currently working on several other adaptations of SNK properties. The studio is producing a Fatal Fury movie written by David S. Goyer (Man of Steel, Foundation, The Dark Knight trilogy) and a Samurai Shodown film, with Laeta Laogridis (Altered Carbon, Alita: Battle Angel, Shutter Island) handling the screenplay. The studio is also backing an Art of Fighting webtoon by digital creator Brandon Chen.

According to recent reports, in 2022, the EGDC, owned by the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation, acquired a 96.18% stake in SNK. As for the studio producing the new Metal Slug film, The Arena is owned by MBC Group, a Saudi media conglomerate, and the Misk Foundation, also known as the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that the Saudi government’s purchase of Electronic Arts and backing of a film studio tie into broader efforts to invest in entertainment products, such as sports leagues, video games, movies, and more. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) recently acquired EA alongside Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners and Silver Lake. The PIF also has stakes in companies such as Capcom, Nintendo, and Take-Two, as well as ownership in e-sports events like the fighting game tournament EVO.

Sources indicate that as for why Saudi investments in the video game industry have proven controversial, these acquisitions have been criticized as a type of “sportswashing,” a method of sanitizing the Saudi government’s image on the world stage by associating itself with “fun” topics, like soccer and golf, instead of human rights abuses. The Saudi government has been accused of exploitation of migrant laborers, enforcement of anti-LGBTQ laws, and the killing of political opponents, such as the alleged murder of Washington Post journalist Jamal Khashoggi. Basically, the Saudi Arabian government would much rather you think about a movie adaptation of that nostalgic game series you used to love instead of these many accusations, all while you contribute to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's war chest.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Even to this day, there's a debate over whether or not "Star Trek: The Animated Series" counts as a canonical installment in the "Star Trek" franchise.
  • Industry observers note that that said, there are aspects of "The Animated Series" that directly contradict other entries in the franchise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Even to this day, there's a debate over whether or not "Star Trek: The Animated Series" counts as a canonical installment in the "Star Trek" franchise. The show ran for 22 episodes over the course of two seasons from 1973 to 1974, and, in certain respects, it's actually better than "The Original Series." Being an animated 30-minute show, it's a lot more efficient in its storytelling and is able to visually realize far more expansive and outlandish ideas. For instance, it features aliens that evolved from plants and an episode that takes place largely underwater.

Industry observers note that that said, there are aspects of "The Animated Series" that directly contradict other entries in the franchise. Take "The Counter-Clock Incident," an episode that introduces Commodore Robert April (James Doohan) as an elderly white man. However, when the character reappeared on "Star Trek: Strange Fresh Worlds," he was played by Adrian Holmes, a Black actor. Then there's the episode "The Magicks of Megas-Tu," which is about the USS Enterprise traveling to the center of the galaxy and encountering a being believed to be the Devil. The thing is, this clashes with the film "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier," in which the Enterprise's crew meets an entity thought to be God at the center of the galaxy.

According to the oral history book "The Fifty-Year Mission," edited by Mark Altman and Edward Gross, "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry himself even said that "The Animated Series" isn't strictly canon. Yet, a lot of the show has become canon over time, as some of the people who worked on it discussed in the short documentary "Drawn to the Final Frontier" (itself included on the series' DVD release).

Sources indicate that it should immediately be pointed out that "Star Trek: The Animated Series" was penned by many of the same writers who worked on "Star Trek: The Original Series," was created by Gene Roddenberry, and features most of the actors from "The Original Series" to boot (save for Walter Koenig as Chekov). What's more, in "Drawn to the Final Frontier," longtime "Trek" writer D.C. Fontana noted that "The Animated Series" had a research tech giant to ensure it aligned with the events of "The Original Series." As she put it, "It has to follow. It has to make sense. They have to agree.".

In a recent development, expanding on this, "The Magicks of Megas-Tu" writer Larry Brody addressed the canon question directly in "Drawn to the Final Frontier," stating, "My take as to whether this fits into the 'Star Trek' legacy is that it fits into my version of the 'Star Trek' legacy. I think it should!" Meanwhile, "The Original Series" and "The Animated Series" writer David Gerrold mentioned he felt that debates about canon are silly:.

"All this argument about canon is stupid. It has Gene Roddenberry's name on it. It has William Shatner as Kirk, it has Leonard Nimoy as Spock, it has [DeForest] Kelley as McCoy, it has Jimmy Doohan as Scotty, it has Majel Barrett as Nurse Chapel, it has Nichelle Nichols as Uhura, it has George Takei as Sulu.".

Likewise, when "The Animated Series" initially aired, it didn't really undermine what had been laid down by "The Original Series." Rather, it was the "Star Trek" highlights and movies that came after it that led to problems. That sounds like canon to me.

Indeed, many details from "Star Trek: The Animated Series" have since found their way into the live-action canon, like how James Kirk's middle name is Tiberius (as he clarifies in the "Animated Series" episode "Bem"). And though presented as a novel invention on "Star Trek: The Next Generation," the holodeck first appeared in the "Animated Series" episode "The Practical Joker.".

Recent findings suggest that in keeping with this, the show "Star Trek: Enterprise" incorporates several elements of "The Animated Series" into the mix. Specifically, a Sehlat — a Vulcan creature that serves as Spock's childhood pet in the "Animated Series" episode "Yesteryear" — appears in the "Enterprise" episode "The Forge." The "Enterprise" episode "The Catwalk" similarly confirms that Vulcans go on a desert-bound maturation ritual when they are children known as the kahs-wan, a term that was first spoken in, you guessed it, "Yesteryear.".

And that's to mention nothing of the animated show "Star Trek: Lower Decks," which integrates myriad details and Easter eggs alluding to "The Animated Series." The latter show may be somewhat forgotten these days, but it's certainly worth revisiting (or watching for the very first time) and remains central to so much of the rest of the "Star Trek" mythology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 2021, at the recommendation of a film producer, the writer and showrunner Rebecca Cutter read a pulpy murder-mystery novel on a flight from her native Massachusetts to her current base in Los Angeles. By the time she landed, Cutter had finished the book and was already mapping out the TV adaptation in her head.

In a recent development, the plot heavily involved a Texas abortion clinic, and the state had just passed SB 8, one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bills until Roe v. Wade was overturned the following year. As she contemplated bringing The Hunting Wives to life, Cutter saw the political stakes come into focus as well.

Sources indicate that “I started thinking about the ‘red state, blue state’ of it,” she tells Vanity Fair ahead of the show’s season two premiere on Thursday. “What if…we really play this culture war?”.

In a recent development, “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes,” says showrunner Rebecca Cutter. “I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.”.

In a recent development, the result was one of Netflix’s biggest breakout hits in recent years, sent up in a Saturday Night Live sketch as the “straight but lesbian, horny Republican murder drama.” As a show, Hunting Wives amps up the noirish aspects of the suspense thriller written by May Cobb, a native of the East Texas Piney Woods, and adds a heaping dose of MAGA-adjacent camp. Cutter finishes the mix with plenty of sex scenes, particularly between Malin Akerman’s Margo, a femme fatale partly inspired by Melania Trump who is married to a Republican gubernatorial hopeful, and Brittany Snow’s Sophie, a liberal do-gooder who, like Cutter, arrives in town from a blue corner of Massachusetts. (Cutter was raised in Cambridge and graduated from Wesleyan University, the Connecticut liberal arts college known for its progressive politics and pipeline to Hollywood.).

Hunting Wives executive producer Erwin Stoff told Cutter he’d pay for her to go to Texas to meet Cobb and breathe the Piney Woods air herself. She met Cobb’s father and her best friend from high school. She shot skeet with the women—she even got it in three, just as Sophie does in the first season. At a high-end Dallas shopping area where the likes of Gucci can be found, Cutter got a better sense of the hair, clothes, and bodies of her eventual characters. “I understand the notion that Sophie could be amused and entertained and intrigued by these women,” Cutter indicates, “and eventually seduced.”.

In a recent development, cutter thinks of the show primarily in terms of its tonal mash-up: “I think we managed to wrangle it into one piece of art,” she claims, “but there’s comedy, there’s violence, there’s noir, there’s soap, there’s earnest emotion.” To the extent that she assigned any political beliefs to the rich white women of Cobb’s novel, it was in the spirit of grounding her characters in the specifics of their world. Still, as we speak, Cutter decides “to get real with it.”.

In a recent development, cutter on set. She describes Sophie, a fellow native of blue Massachusetts, as a surrogate for her own awakening to MAGA Texas.

In a recent development, “The whole thing was a little bit of a parable, in my mind, of how you could fall for someone like [Donald] Trump,” she admits. “Sophie has her principles, but they only go so far. They end right where something starts to make her feel good.” Cutter was as curious as anyone else from her educated milieu about the quirkier aspects of Trump, like the Diet Coke button he had installed on the Resolute Desk. How liberating must it feel to embrace a movement so openly untethered from the pieties of politics and taste?

“Not that my show is a deep dive on Trump,” Cutter states, “but maybe there is an element that’s sort of looking under the hood.”.

The twisted love story between Margo and Sophie entangles all of the wealthy, hard-drinking, gun-toting women in their orbit, and its central killing—one of several propelling the show forward, with a third season slated to begin filming this year—stems from an effort to cover up Margo’s abortion as her NRA-loving husband plots his political ascent. (In this proudly oversexed town, he has his own share of affairs.) Hunting Wives is the rare Netflix soap to receive steady coverage from mainstream national outlets; the fascination undoubtedly has something to do with the impression that, like Yellowstone or Morgan Wallen before it, the show unlocks something about MAGA’s cultural staying power. In a Fresh York Times guest essay this month that evaluated the post-2024 Hollywood landscape, Sharon Waxman, the editor in chief of The Wrap, wrote, “From Melania on Amazon’s streaming service to The Hunting Wives on Netflix to the ever-expanding Taylor Sheridan universe on Paramount+ to Bari Weiss’s being put in charge of CBS News, the vibe shift was visible on all our screens.”.

Margo and her politically ambitious husband are partners in subterfuge and debauchery.

Cutter says she had no particular agenda nor any “ultra-evil villain blueprint of how it was going to be received or how it would be culturally relevant.” But Hunting Wives is sprinkled with enough proper nouns—a Peter Thiel mention here, a Walmart reference there—and distinctly modern aesthetics that she can acknowledge its appeal as something of a Rosetta stone for the moment in MAGA femininity. Even in the ostensibly waning days of the movement, the plastic surgery and soaring heels continue to captivate and horrify coastal elites. Cutter says that Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), another of Margo’s lovers, has a bit of Kristi Noem and Marjorie Taylor Greene in her: that “sort of slightly butch, real gun, real ‘back the blue’ [element]…the toughness of those women.”.

It has been revealed that the second season of Hunting Wives maintains the slipperiness that keeps the show from veering into moralism; it stands apart from other Trump-era art in its refusal to take sides. “I think I remember, in the pitch, someone saying, ‘But will red-state people like it too?’” Cutter recalls. “I was like, ‘I think so.’” Both Margo and Sophie are awash in their respective red and blue stereotypes, but neither is more admirable than the other. Their sordid union is a testament to the flexibility of both their principles and their preferences. From one vantage, it is, in the end, all about sex.

In a recent development, “Margo is the symbol of freedom and sexuality and feminine power and empoweredness and selfishness that [Sophie] feels she’s lost,” Cutter states, adding that Akerman’s comfort in such a role helped drive her liberal use of physical intimacy. “The audience may disagree with me,” she says, but “I don’t think I do gratuitous sex scenes. I think you always are seeing a power dynamic play out or a plot point play out.” Last year, though, when Netflix acquired Hunting Wives, which was initially ordered by Starz in 2023, Cutter had a more practical concern.

“I literally googled,” she recalls, “‘Does Netflix show boobs?’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss has made headlines for multiple reasons since being hired for the job in October 2025, but one specific aspect of the job she continues to receive backlash for is 60 Minutes. This past summer, Weiss and executive producer Nick Bilton cut ties with several high-profile employees and, more recently, the show has seen losses in viewership. Now, some fresh numbers regarding the news magazine show’s 59th season have arrived, and they mark yet another setback for Weiss and her staff.

Going into this latest season of 60 Minutes, which premiered in September amid the 2026 TV schedule, there was much speculation as to how the show would fare ratings-wise. This latest Nielsen data update from The Wall Street Journal (via The Independent) suggests that the show has indeed been underperforming with its broadcasts. Per the report, the series averaged 8.3 million viewers for the nine episodes that aired between September 9 and November 16. That marks a 16 percent drop from the previous season.

Recent findings suggest that months ago, Season 59 premiered to 6.5 million viewers on CBS, and that sum differed from the initial report of 7.7 million (which was not finalized at the time). One of the key commonalities between both reports, however, is that the news program has seen losses within the 25-54 demographic. In that demo, 60 has apparently seen a 25 percent decline compared to last season. This demographic is critical, especially when considering on-air advertising.

Recent findings suggest that these ratings mark another less-than-desired situation for CBS News during what’s been a major year of change for 60 Minutes. In May, correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were fired along with executive producer Tanya Simon and several others. Just recently, Vega stated she found it “disturbing” that she still didn’t know the exact reason she was let go. And, shortly after those moves were made, Scott Pelley was also fired from the show after allegedly accusing Weiss of “murdering” the series.

Sources indicate that another topic of discussion revolves around the claims of “journalistic interference” at 60. Series alums like Pelley and Vega have alleged that they were encouraged to insert what they considered to be news bias into their reporting. CBS veteran Dan Rather also chastised Weiss and co. for their reporting. The E-I-C has denied that employees’ editorial autonomy has been taken away from journalists at the company.

With the team at 60 Minutes being aware of the chatter that’s surrounded the show as of late, Bari Weiss recently addressed concerns. She recently spoke at a conference organized by The Information, where she stated the show had been doing “tremendously well.” She also emphasized that her main objective for CBS News as a whole was to build a news media organization built on trust. In doing so, she’s made changes to several programs, with the aforementioned show really receiving a makeover.

Sources indicate that bari Weiss Apparently ‘Arrived Like A Conquering Hero’ At CBS News. Why Things Reportedly Changed.

After parting ways with Pelley and co., Weiss hired several other broadcasters to fill out 60 Minutes’ new broadcasting team. Ross Douthat, Gianna Toboni, Sebastian Junger, Sir Trevor Phillips and Ariel Levy were ultimately brought on. Those newcomers are now working alongside the show’s three on-camera veterans: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim. Just recently, Stahl addressed the backlash she faced due to remaining with the show under Weiss’ leadership and noted she did so in order for the series as they know it not to “vanish.”.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, there may still be some level of continuity from a talent perspective, but the ratings still stand. As of this writing, neither Bari Weiss nor anyone else from CBS News has addressed this latest viewership update on 60 Minutes. Time will tell how Weiss, Nick Bilton and more might seek to remedy the situation.

#85641. Tech Report: Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

Tech Report: Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The other day, one line in an otherwise unremarkable marketing email caught my eye: “Discovery is exactly what fans come to Netflix for.”.
  • Even with a dangling preposition (in a press release littered with errors), the claim felt like the more glaring mistake: Netflix is where fans go for discovery.
  • But when it comes to Netflix’s core business — streaming television — the service is largely a preferred destination by default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day, one line in an otherwise unremarkable marketing email caught my eye: “Discovery is exactly what fans come to Netflix for.”.

Even with a dangling preposition (in a press release littered with errors), the claim felt like the more glaring mistake: Netflix is where fans go for discovery. They do? Still? Are you sure about that?

But when it comes to Netflix’s core business — streaming television — the service is largely a preferred destination by default. Being an industry pioneer helped establish Netflix as a utility among TV fans, many of whom still turn to it when they want to see “what’s on,” but it’s hard to imagine why anyone would head there first when searching for their next favorite show.

It has been revealed that that would require the customer to trust Netflix — either as the service offering the most bang for their buck, the demonstrates everyone is talking about, or, most likely and simplest of all, the best series on TV. Can the streamer really stake a claim to any of those distinctions?

According to recent reports, not anymore. Not after this year.

It has been revealed that throughout 2026, Netflix has been plagued by problems and complaints. Viewership for returning seasons is dwindling, subscription prices are rising, hot newly introduced franchises are scarce, and high-quality programming — a subjective designation, to be sure — isn’t what it used to be. Netflix is no longer the most affordable SVOD service. It’s not the most award-winning, nor is it the buzziest.

Recent findings suggest that A sustainable hit could quiet things down, but those have been hard to come by. Netflix’s most popular new shows this year were limited series (like “His & Hers” and “I Will Find You”), which only offer short-term juice. Promising first seasons (“The Boroughs”) faced quick cancellations that left fans fuming and analysts searching for answers. Even touted chart toppers (“Man on Fire”) don’t get a quick Season 2 renewal, let alone a quick turnaround between seasons.

Ignoring these very-online narratives, none of the aforementioned demonstrates earned rave reviews, and the streamer’s awards output echoed what’s felt like a dearth in quality. Total Emmy wins were cut nearly in half this year, from 30 to 16, causing Netflix to fall to third place (behind HBO and Apple) for the first time since topping the town in 2021.

According to recent reports, A month after Emmy night, all the criticism reached a crescendo when a plunging stock price and lack of hits forced mass layoffs, including the dismissal of chief content officer Bela Bajaria and other key executives. Peter Rice is at the helm now, and his latest team is setting the table for changes in 2027 — much like Netflix did in 2022 after The Great Streaming Correction opened the door for an ad-tier and shut the door on password sharing.

Sources indicate that while it would be foolish to believe fixing one aspect of a diverse business would make all its other problems go away, it would be equally foolish to pretend there’s not a TV problem at Netflix. A healthy TV slate only benefits engagement across the platform, and the streamer is still the massive dog in SVOD — it’s just losing ground year by year. So what’s to be done?

Well, that depends on how much Netflix is willing to change. If it’s all on the table, there are a handful of reasonable shifts they could make to improve their reputation. If not, well, I’ve got an idea for that, too.

Industry observers note that at the root of Netflix’s TV problem is that its indicates feel disposable. Sometimes that’s by design: Netflix makes a lot of programs that can be watched while scrolling, which can be OK. TV has long been a medium built for background entertainment, and it’s still nice to have an easily digestible distraction while doing dishes or folding laundry.

But Netflix may have gone too far. Setting aside quality (for a moment), the streamer’s focus on “discovery” paired with its faith in the almighty algorithm to sort through its substantial monthly programming influx emphasizes upcoming demonstrates above all else. There’s always another new series, new special, or new live event to watch, but there isn’t always more of the show you already love. Some original series take years between releasing new seasons. Some only dole out six or eight episodes every 18 months. Some get canceled after one or two seasons, and very few run more than three or four seasons in total.

Whether or not the approach works from a financial perspective, it fails to foster audience investment, and investment is where TV thrives. Just look at this year’s most-watched highlights on streaming, per Nielsen: “Stranger Things” holds down the No. 1 spot, but then it’s “Bluey,” “The Pitt,” “Grey’s Anatomy,” and “The Big Bang Theory.” Keep scrolling and it’s even easier to spot the dominant trend: Shows with huge libraries that first aired on network TV.

Recent findings suggest that these are the kind of reveals that people keep up with for years, decades, or more. They like the characters, they like the structure, they like the setting — they like being in the show’s world, whether it’s a hospital filled with hot doctors or a nerd’s living room. Offering access on a regular basis encourages investment, which breeds loyalty, which creates longevity. Producing more episodes, more often — like broadcast TV has done all along — creates bigger libraries that fans will happily live in for years on end because they enjoy spending time with those characters and within those stories.

Recent findings suggest that streamers have been reluctant to adopt their predecessor’s production model (for reasons both valid and ridiculous that I’ll get into in the next section), but the success of long-running (and long-gone) broadcast series on streaming, paired with the recent popularity of “The Pitt,” makes it hard to argue against making longer seasons, consisting of more episodes, that are released on a regular basis. It’s what audiences want now, and it’s what they’ve shown they’ll want later.

Which brings us to the binge model. One of the reasons Netflix hasn’t experimented with more broadcast-style streaming shows (like “The Pitt”) is because it can’t. Its release model is different. The binge model requires everything be done before anything premieres, including timely post-production work like subtitles and dubbing, which Netflix needs to serve its global base. While episodes of most network series are still being written, shot, and edited as earlier, completed episodes roll out, episodes of a Netflix series drop all at once.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, Netflix already made the change. Or started to, at least.

Nowadays, Netflix’s most popular original series are often released in batches (or “parts”), including the last two seasons of “Stranger Things” and “Bridgerton.” Both demonstrates are among the most-watched programs on the planet, so the shift in release strategy hasn’t hurt their popularity. Other shows are already released weekly, like “The Great British Baking Show,” or close to weekly, like “Love Is Blind.”.

Industry observers note that moreover, the addition of live events has forced Netflix to implement new tactics to raise awareness for time-sensitive content (instead of just relying on the algorithm), which should limit fears over viewer confusion. (For seasons released in parts, the Netflix platform tends to list how many episodes will be released and when. You can even set reminders for upcoming programming, even if none of it is available yet — like, say, the NFL game on Thanksgiving Eve, which is a thing, I guess.).

Sources indicate that netflix decided long ago to break up the binge, now they just need to keep going. After all, the binge model was created to disrupt Hollywood. No one was releasing full seasons at once, and Netflix executives recognized how DVDs had primed viewers to marathon TV demonstrates. Instead of old favorites (like “The Office”), why not give them new ones to devour?

It has been revealed that but Netflix isn’t a disruptor anymore. It’s the industry leader. It doesn’t need a gimmick to draw attention. It needs a strategy to help keep it.

According to recent reports, A weekly release model could help. Netflix doesn’t need to enforce it on every series — let people binge “Ginny & Georgia” — but for reveals that could benefit from the regular cycle of anticipation, fulfillment, dissection (repeat), the tried-and-true strategy could do wonders for audience investment. In the short-term, it could help prevent dips in engagement and help foster engagement with newly beloved series. In the long-term, it could help build franchises, libraries, and loyalty.

You can’t just make the next “Pitt.” You have to create the system to support it.

Speaking of support, it’s time to talk about quality. What constitutes a good show and a bad show will always, in the end, remain in the eye of the beholder, but a company aiming to “replace all television” can’t rely on subjective interpretations to define its brand. Nor can it rely primarily on an algorithm to elevate the best options instead of the easiest ones. Otherwise, you risk a narrative like this year’s, where objective measurements like ratings (where the three most-watched new demonstrates average a 56 rating on Metacritic) and awards (where Netflix landed one more win than NBC and Peacock combined) create the impression of less-than-“gourmet” service.

Some such schemes are already underway with pre-show ads running before episodes and prominent brand campaigns helping connect viewers with their new favorite programs. Hopefully, that signals more old-school advocacy efforts are coming. Eventize episodes, not just new seasons. Build channels for episodic programs to elevate their best moments. Add permanent subsections to Netflix’s genre listings.

This is not a fresh idea. At various times for various reasons, various experts have suggested Netflix launch a free subscription tier in order to promote its growing library to a wider audience. FAST (free, ad-supported streaming) platforms like Pluto, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are growing promptly mainly by replicating the broadcast model for the streaming age, and Netflix could take a page out of their playbook to expand their business in any number of ways. But in terms of solving their TV problem, they should use it to distinguish their premium original programming from their recent obsession: YouTube slop.

I’ll be honest: I don’t think of Netflix and YouTube as competitors, mainly because Netflix isn’t free. Sure, there’s YouTube Premium, but YouTube is instantly accessible, sans subscription, and that’s how most users get hooked. I don’t care how many more hours people spend watching YouTube than Netflix because the hours I spend watching movie trailers, how-to-videos, and late-night clips are not the same as the hours I spend watching “Little House on the Prairie,” “Long Story Short,” and “East of Eden.” One I’m willing to pay for, one I’m not. So the idea that Netflix, as a business, should be trying to surpass YouTube never made sense to me.

Recent findings suggest that it still doesn’t, but I understand the market demands constant growth, and I understand why Netflix would want YouTube’s viewers, especially in the younger demographic. So Netflix has been busy signing content creators, adding podcasts, and filling the service with easy-listening videos (aka videos you don’t need to watch, but can play in the background without much disturbance). If that helps bring the next generation to Netflix so they can discover the glory of “BoJack Horseman,” great! But right now, BoJack is sitting side by side with random content like “Conspiracy Theories,” “Small Town Murder,” and “Bill Simmons.”.

In a recent development, that’s a problem. We shouldn’t equate those very distinct experiences, and Netflix shouldn’t suggest we do. At best, it builds a false equivalency that steadily lowers our artistic standards for visual entertainment. At worst, it leads to more fans of this “Bill Simmons.”.

So let’s create some tiers. Launch a free version of Netflix where all the podcasts, creator videos, and short-form content can live. Make money the old-fashioned way — from ads — while offering select TV highlights to sample in the hopes viewers will get hooked and pay for an upgraded subscription. Keep original series, movies, and other top library offerings on the paid tiers, and structure those however you like. (Presently, there’s Standard with Ads, Standard, and Premium, each with their distinct perks.).

Is creating a FAST version of Netflix a whole lot of work to dispel the notion that Netflix makes too much disposable TV? Yup, and I won’t pretend to know how feasible it is, financially or otherwise. But Netflix needs to take a substantial swing or two if it hopes to fix its reputation, which brings us to my last option.

In a recent development, netflix is still the dominant streamer in Hollywood. Plentiful stats support its case, but why look any further than how many other streamers license content to their biggest competitor? Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, and more each lend their once-exclusive series to their rival in the hope of getting the Netflix bump (or a quick influx of cash). Never did I think I’d see the day where HBO would be available on another streamer, and yet everything from “Sex and the City” to “Ballers” has graced Netflix in 2026.

Industry observers note that with that in mind, Netflix may choose to stay the course. The once-and-future tech tech giant is notorious for sticking to certain brand tenets, like trusting the algorithm over traditional marketing and its binge model over traditional release strategies. Even when Hollywood pushes back, Netflix’s broader goals continue to evolve. Originally, it wanted to be the HBO of streaming. Then it wanted to replace cable. Then it wanted to replace all television.

What it wants to be now isn’t so clear. Wall Street keeps forcing comparisons to YouTube, some of which are invited by Netflix’s pursuit of its content and podcast creators. Maybe Netflix executives believe they can raise their market cap with vertical videos and video game previews, with fresh decision-makers and added theatrical grosses, with a few small tweaks here and a few surprise wins there. It has the leverage to wait out complaints and keep making TV exactly as it has been, if it so chooses.

Sources indicate that but because of its relative health, I hope Netflix sees its TV problem as more of a TV opportunity. Yes, it needs more hits. Yes, it needs to build back trust. But it also wants to grow, and the suggestions above are all about sustainable growth through better TV. Longer seasons, more episodes, weekly releases, stronger support, clearer delineations, a FAST service — none of these ideas are revolutionary. They’re not meant to be. They’re meant to give the people what they want.

If Netflix is going to be where fans go for discovery, it first needs to be a place they can trust to get what what they need.

According to recent reports, here it was, the big reveal. After years of planning and wrangling, after more than $10 million spent on engineers and lawyers and architects, after all of the rumors and headlines and finger-pointing, the long-awaited presentation was ready to be made.

About 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails. A “shitshow,” as multiple people would later describe to Vanity Fair the two-and-a-half-hour meeting on the morning of July 29.

It has been revealed that the setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at New York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner. Seated at round tables were 40 or so of the people with enough disposable income to call the Pierre home, or at least a home: investor Austin Hearst; Tory Burch, the fashion powerhouse; Lois Chiles, the 1970s-era movie star and model. Joining remotely was Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, who last year spent $4.3 million to buy a second apartment there and, with it, even more shares in the co-op that owns the Pierre.

In came representatives from the Khashoggi Holding Organization out of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and the Dorchester Collection, the luxury hotel management firm owned by the Sultan of Brunei. Their proposition was straightforward. Khashoggi wanted to buy the Pierre—the nearly 200-room hotel and all of the apartments too—for $2 billion, less expenses. It was an enormous haul, even for a neighborhood this tony. And it would be all in cash. “The funds are currently available,” a Khashoggi representative promised.

According to recent reports, but if the residents with two thirds of the co-op’s shares accepted the offer, everyone would have to move out. Neighbors would be voting, in effect, to force their fellow neighbors from their apartments.

Industry observers note that it would be in their best interest, the Dorchester and Khashoggi reps remarked. The Pierre was a gem, but a tarnished one after 96 summers and thousands of guests. It didn’t have many of the amenities that come standard these days in a five-star hotel. The façade was already undergoing a $22 million overhaul, and there were deeper, systemic problems to solve. The CEO of the manufacturer managing the Pierre publicly complained it was something of a money pit. All of that would change after Khashoggi bought the place, the presenters promised. Dorchester would invest more than $1 billion into the Pierre, giving the landmark building a grand new entrance on 61st Street, a pool in the basement, and structural renovations throughout.

When it was done, the residents would be first in line to buy apartments at the all-new, all-modern Dorchester-managed Pierre, ready to last another century.

In a recent development, the response in the Cotillion room was instant and not particularly friendly. Some residents had moved in not long ago. Others had spent millions remodeling their apartments. “How are we going to enjoy all the perks of this wonderfully renewed building when we’re forced to sell at a price you determine and we have to buy reconfigured apartments, not our own, at market prices?” asked Tina Beriro, the philanthropist and longtime resident, in a recording of the meeting reviewed by Vanity Fair. Like many of the residents, Beriro, at 85, was only a few years younger than the hotel itself. “Many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”.

Sources indicate that christopher Cowdray, Dorchester’s white-haired, Zimbabwe-born president, didn’t have an answer. Nor did he provide much of a response when asked what would happen to the more than 400 people who work at the hotel. “In this case, we are still in discussion at the moment,” Cowdray said, to audible groans.

It has been revealed that “Many employees have worked here 30 and 40 years and are just about to hit retirement,” Burch pointed out, per the recording. “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line.”.

Industry observers note that the questions kept coming. For years, shareholders had begged—and even sued—to find out more about the sale. But the long-promised detailed aims for the Pierre’s purchase were still weeks away, adding to the tension in the Cotillion room. (One source, very much in favor of a sale, later called the decision to make an elaborate presentation to the shareholders without those specifics “idiotic.”).

“Look, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been on the board of the Hearst Corporation for over 25 years. Sat on the boards of many corporations, for profit and not for profit. I have never seen anything like this,” Hearst said, his voice cracking. “This is a serious problem that you have presented to the shareholders, and you guys have done a miserable fucking job.”.

Industry observers note that one of the many lawyers in the room interrupted him, and they started going at it. Cowdray and the other presenters were escorted out. At one point, the wife of Michael Stern, the 88-year-old chairman of the co-op’s board, tried to offer his resignation on his behalf (which he then turned down). Even by the famously hostile standards of Fresh York City’s high-end co-ops, this was nasty.

It has been revealed that ironically, the co-op’s biggest shareholder—the resident with the most at stake in the sale financially—didn’t show up. Howard Lutnick was busy in the Oval Office that day with President Donald Trump in his role as US commerce secretary.

Lutnick had bought the Pierre’s 16-room penthouse, its largest apartment, in 2017 for $44 million. If the sale of the Pierre were to go through, Lutnick would get as much as $100 million for the penthouse, even as his neighbors were forced to sell and hundreds of hotel staffers’ jobs were put in jeopardy. Newmark Group—the real estate services firm hired by the Pierre’s board and controlled by Cantor Fitzgerald, the brokerage house previously run by Lutnick—would earn tens of millions more.

Sources indicate that newmark may have a reputation for shepherding substantial-ticket sales to completion. But in a letter to the Pierre’s board last year, Beriro called the hiring of the Lutnick-linked firm “a blatant conflict of interest,” an allegation sources close to Lutnick and the board deny. One Pierre resident tells me that Lutnick’s involvement is symbolic of a “culture of corruption” that extends from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington to the edges of Central Park in Fresh York. Others imply it is part of a different pattern: the purchase of more and more of America’s most valuable assets by companies and sovereign wealth funds from the Persian Gulf’s petrostates, at times orchestrated by those in and around the second Trump administration. Those shareholders wonder whether Lutnick had personally worked behind the scenes to maneuver the Khashoggi group into place to buy the Pierre, and that speculation spilled onto the pages of The New York Times.

BALL GAMES Guests attend a Valentino party in the Cotillion Ballroom at the Pierre hotel, 1970, Upcoming York.

Recent findings suggest that A source close to Lutnick notes that he formally cut ties with Newmark in early 2025 and adds that, since his move to government, Lutnick’s only involvement in the Pierre sales process has been to respond to media reports like this one. A spokesperson for Sabre Park Avenue LLC, Khashoggi’s American holding company, tells Vanity Fair in a statement that “any insinuation or implication that the proposal, the transaction or the parties involved engaged in improper or undisclosed conduct is categorically false.”.

I spoke to more than 15 sources and reviewed hundreds of pages of documents related to the Pierre deal, including previously unreported text messages between Lutnick and Khashoggi and a corporate intelligence dossier dropped in my mailbox.

Turns out, the shareholders were right to wonder about Lutnick’s role.

Industry observers note that the Pierre for decades was synonymous with New York glamour. At the height of their star power, Audrey Hepburn stayed in the hotel’s suites and Elizabeth Taylor kept an apartment there. The restaurant’s original menu was created by Escoffier. Barbara Walters had a reception for her final wedding at the Pierre (about 10 years after she and my grandfather, the Broadway producer Lee Guber, officially split). Yves Saint Laurent owned a two-bedroom on the 38th floor, which was later bought by Valentino cofounder Giancarlo Giammetti, who then sold it to former Bottega Veneta creative director Tomas Maier.

According to recent reports, and yet for 15 years or more, there’s been a growing sense that the Pierre’s best days are behind it, even as the stars continue to use the hotel to get ready for the Met Gala. A 2010 Wall Street Journal article mentions how the Pierre “lost its glory.” By the time Lutnick swooped in to buy the penthouse in 2017, he did so at an $81 million discount off its original asking price.

THE TORY PARTY Fashion designer Tory Burch, in one of the hotel’s elevators, was among the residents opposed to the sale.

Since then, age has continued to take its toll. Scaffolding has surrounded the hotel since at least 2018, according to city records. Exit a multimillion-dollar apartment with a spectacular view of the park and you’re liable to find worn carpets or hallways with the faint odor of mold. Rooms at the Pierre tend to cost much less than they do at the Plaza or the Ritz-Carlton, just around the corner.

According to recent reports, over time, a group of shareholders became particularly vexed with Taj Hotels, which had managed the property since 2005. There were complaints of broken elevators, empty concierge desks, and “slipshod maintenance.” Maier, in an October 2023 co-op-wide email, lamented that Taj delayed long-planned renovations to his apartment for months, citing high hotel occupancy. (A Taj spokesperson said in a statement those concerns “reflected a specific point in time rather than the overall trajectory of the property.”).

In a recent development, what Maier may not have known—and what the residents I spoke to were unaware of—was that the Pierre’s board had already explored the possibility of replacing Taj. The only way to do that, to break the contract with Taj, was to sell the Pierre. In April 2023, the board drafted a memorandum of understanding with the Maybourne Hotel Group, which is primarily owned by members of the Qatari royal family, to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre. “But there was a condition,” a source familiar with the matter tells me. “Everybody had to move out for two years.” The source adds, “You cannot renovate a 100-year-old building with people living in it, right?”.

That was a deal killer. So the board decided, in this source’s words, to hire a firm that could broker a “more acceptable” sale. They picked the real estate consultancy Newmark. Lutnick was still chairman of Newmark’s board at that time, though two sources say he had no role in the decision. (The board, through its attorney, declined to comment for this story. But a Newmark spokesperson states its “unanimous” selection was “based on the firm’s experience advising on some of New York City’s most complex and high-profile real estate transactions.”).

From there, “Newmark went out to find another buyer,” the first source adds. Its fee at the time: $50,000 per month, to be counted against any future commissions in the event of a sale. (Eventually that was bargained down to a flat $30 million.) The board retained the high-profile law firm Fried Frank, which had represented Lutnick’s companies before, to assist Newmark in its search.

LONDON'S CALLING Christopher Cowdray, the Dorchester Collection’s president, was part of the contentious presentation to residents in the Cotillion ballroom at the Pierre.

Industry observers note that since Lutnick’s financial firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, owned a controlling stake in Newmark, that gave Lutnick an incentive to see the Pierre sold. He had another: According to the source connected to Lutnick, his 12,000-square-foot penthouse triplex had been uninhabitable since 2021, when a storm had caused catastrophic damage. Lutnick concluded, according to the source close to him, that major repairs wouldn’t make sense if they weren’t accompanied by a larger round of structural renovations to the building. In the meantime, he installed a basketball court in the apartment to make some use of the place.

When the sales process started, the idea was to make a deal for the hotel only. The upcoming owner would likely want to consolidate guest rooms on certain floors. That meant some Pierre residents might be encouraged—strongly encouraged—to sell, but not necessarily everyone.

In a recent development, brokers approached everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to Michael Dell to the king of Morocco to buy the place. Most of the residents were in the dark. As far as they knew, Newmark was trying to help renovate the building, not sell it off. Nor did they know Lutnick was personally trying to wrangle potential buyers for the Pierre.

In a recent development, on Wednesday, May 8, 2024, Lutnick’s private jet took off from Teterboro, Fresh Jersey, outside of New York. Lutnick was on his way to Paris to meet with the Arnault family who, as part of their dominion over LVMH, run the Cheval Blanc hotel group. The source close to Lutnick mentions he had long admired the hotels and pitched the idea of the Pierre joining the group.

Lutnick’s first stop, however, was in London. After his plane landed, he went to the Dorchester Collection’s eponymous hotel in Mayfair. Shortly after 9 a.m. on Thursday, Lutnick gathered with Cowdray, the Dorchester president, and Motasem Khashoggi, chairman and principal owner of the Khashoggi Holding Tech giant. From the outside, it seemed like an unlikely trio. The Khashoggi family was mainly famous for its wealth, but that was decades ago, back when Adnan, Motasem’s relative, was one of the world’s leading arms dealers. Motasem is recognized internationally today not as a captain of Saudi industry but as the primary legal representative for the Khashoggi family following the brutal 2018 murder of his journalist cousin, Jamal, by the Saudi state.

The source close to Lutnick says he and Khashoggi “met and spoke about a variety of different things” in London, “including: Wouldn’t it be cool if the Pierre was a Dorchester Collection hotel.” Eight days after the London meeting, according to screenshots of WhatsApp messages reviewed by Vanity Fair, Khashoggi texted Lutnick to say that “Brunie”—Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei, who owns the Dorchester Collection—had “directly” asked him to explore a deal for the Pierre.

According to recent reports, khashoggi then asked Lutnick if he could give one of his kids a summer internship and provided his phone number. (Vanity Fair verified that number, as well as the ones used by Lutnick and the elder Khashoggi in the chats.) Lutnick promptly agreed to the father’s request. “We would be delighted to have your son join us,” he wrote. “I’m excited to invest in and build exciting companies together.”.

A week later, Khashoggi sent the chat his greetings “from rainy Frankfurt,” along with a draft letter of intent to the Pierre’s board to begin due diligence for a “potential acquisition of The Pierre Hotel” and a plan to buy up “the remaining residential units.”.

Industry observers note that lutnick wrote back on Memorial Day. “I am flying to Europe this evening, Italy and France,” he texted. “I’ve made a few modifications to the letter of intent.” Promise a “complete renovation of the guest rooms, public areas, dining facilities, and amenities,” Lutnick suggested. And be sure to include target prices, both per room and for the whole thing.

Lutnick’s firm, Newmark, was supposed to be representing the sellers in this transaction. Yet here Lutnick was coaching potential buyers, in effect putting himself on both sides of the deal. It wasn’t a cardinal sin in the take-no-prisoners worlds of New York City real estate or MAGA politics, but it wasn’t strictly kosher either.

In a recent development, lutnick was confirmed as commerce secretary in February 2025; he stepped down from his Newmark chairmanship then and transferred his Cantor Fitzgerald assets to his sons. Lutnick was still listed as a member of the Pierre’s “transaction committee” in March, when the board confirmed in a letter that Newmark was in negotiations with an unnamed “operator.” But not to worry, the board added: “No owner would be required to sell their unit or move to another one.”.

Sources indicate that residents scrambled to find out more. All they got back were rumors and whispers. One shareholder’s representative notes he heard the chatter but “blew it off,” thinking that nervous residents were being “dramatic.” According to this representative, the attorneys at Holland & Knight, which had represented the Pierre for years, seemed to be in the dark as well. “You can’t sell a co-op. Never happening here,” one of those lawyers told the representative in this source’s recounting. (Holland & Knight declined to comment for this story.).

In June 2025, the New York Post reported that the Sultan of Brunei was in talks to buy the Pierre, along with Essam ­Khashoggi, an older relative of Motasem’s. The board, chaired by Michael Stern, didn’t provide many specifics in a July Zoom with shareholders but emphasized that a sale was in their best interest, according to multiple published accounts. Two months later, according to court filings, four co-op board members—the investor John Levin, former Coca-Cola CEO Douglas Daft, the lawyer and movie producer David G. Johnson, and former KB Home chief executive Bruce Karatz—approved a nonbinding term sheet to sell the Pierre.

Recent findings suggest that on September 16, at a gathering in the Cotillion Ballroom, Fried Frank lawyers broke the news to shareholders. Khashoggi Holding was the buyer, and the sultan’s Dorchester Collection would be the hotel’s managers. The price was astronomical, they remarked, and would guarantee residents “at least three times the market value” for their apartments, Town & Country reported. But the transaction was different from the one discussed back in March. It was not just for the hotel and selected apartments. It was for the whole building, which meant the co-op owners had to vacate within 12 months. All of them.

BREAKFAST NEAR TIFFANY'S A young woman enjoys room service at the Pierre Hotel, 1943.

In a recent development, an escrow account of $10 million, funded by the shareholders, would be “used for eviction proceedings” for any residents who refused to leave, according to a slideshow presentation delivered by the lawyers that day. And on that happy note, residents were encouraged to open the personalized envelopes that had been given to them at the door, one for each shareholder. Inside were estimates of how much they might get from a sale.

One person who was there states it reminded him of a “game show,” and kind of an insulting one to the ultrarich in the room, for whom a few million dollars either way wouldn’t matter all that much. What was particularly galling, according to sources at the meeting, was the plan for the building’s union employees. Many of them, they stated, were like family—to each other and to the residents. The staff would have to begin to go even sooner. Before Khashoggi would be asked to put down a penny, Fried Frank noted in its presentation, the firm “will engage with the Hotel Gaming and Trades Union to negotiate terms for the termination of the Union Contract.”.

Employees at the Pierre tend to talk about their tenures in decades. “I only have 12 years here,” one staffer tells me without irony. Some ­workers have jobs that are so old-school, they’re not really jobs anywhere else: elevator drivers, telephone switchboard operators. Housekeeping staff wear black-and-white outfits that wouldn’t have been out of place in Audrey Hepburn’s day. “I’m very used to it,” this employee claims, referring to the atmosphere at the Pierre. She means that as a positive.

Like many Pierre staffers, she’s an immigrant. A 2021 New Yorker profile counted “49 languages” spoken by the staff, “including Cantonese, Creole, Danish, Farsi, Greek, Hindi, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Tagalog, Tamil, Tibetan, and Twi.” I spoke with employees who are originally from four different continents.

Recent findings suggest that one was a man I’ll call Ray, who has put in more than a quarter century at the Pierre and would very much like to keep going, even if the severance deal written into his union contract is pretty sweet: Ray figures he could live off of it for a year. But then what? He’s still got kids in school. And at the other hotels in town, the competition for open positions is really intense; promotions come mostly from within. “The chances of getting hired [in his particular department] are almost zero,” Ray tells me. “So I wouldn’t want to get a buyout. I don’t want the hotel to be closed.” Just in case, he’s taken a part-time gig elsewhere.

In a recent development, “We’re not like these millionaires, billionaires, the Howard Lutnicks, the Tory Burches,” notes another Pierre employee. “Just working people, trying to protect their families.”.

The rumors about a sale have been around long enough, and loud enough, that they rattled the staffers I spoke to. Even a renovation could upend staffers’ lives: The remodeling at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel lasted eight years; more than 1,200 union workers were bought out of their contracts. “Most of us, we worry,” a housekeeper tells me.

People move to the Pierre, in part, because of the staff. More than a few residents come to be taken care of, to be treated like five-star hotel guests in their own (second, or third) homes. Room service is available from 6:45 a.m. to 10:45 p.m. Housekeeping comes in seven days a week; the apartments I saw were immaculate in every way, part of the reason why maintenance costs can run tens of thousands of dollars per month. (“I haven’t made a bed since I was a kid,” claims one long-term resident.).

My mom for years talked about retiring to a place like this, not that she could’ve afforded it. For older people who can, it’s a way to have the help they need while still living on their own. You see a lot of women who’ve lost or split up with their rich husbands: Beriro, the philanthropist and animal-rights activist; Gale Hayman, the cofounder of Giorgio’s of Beverly Hills; Mimi Sternlicht, the social entrepreneur; Julie Opperman, the prolific author whose late husband started the Westlaw legal-research service.

You could, perhaps, confuse these women for pushovers, one Belle Vivier pump away from assisted living. At the July meeting, Dorchester and Khashoggi brought gifts for the shareholders: bright-red teddy bears. “For little old ladies to snuggle up to in their beds,” one resident laughs at lunch afterward. Then she grabbed my utensils to cut my food.

Recent findings suggest that these ladies were long past cuddly tchotchkes. Over time, several residents, most of them women and most of them over 65, had formed a loose coalition to learn what they could about the deal for the Pierre and figure ways to stop it. “It was a handful of older women,” the resident adds, “banging on the pipes, saying, ‘Listen up, people!’ ”.

Industry observers note that some of them, at least at first, were open to the idea of a sale; they had other homes, after all. But the cloak of secrecy around the deal infuriated them. So in the days leading up to the contentious reveal of the Khashoggi proposal in September 2025, Chiles and Beriro and others banded together with Hearst and Burch—relative youngsters—and lawyered up. “We became an informal little group: Tory and a bunch of widows,” one source with direct knowledge of the matter indicates, tongue a bit in cheek.

ABOVE BOARD Investor Austin Hearst is part of a group of Pierre residents who sued the co-op board to produce more information about the sale of the building.

Sources indicate that in November 2025, the group sued the board to force it to produce more information about the sale, with Burch’s LLC as the lead plaintiff: how much the board really knew about the buyer; which third parties might benefit from it. Shortly after, Fried Frank lawyer Michael Keats criticized Burch in a letter to her attorney: “this [her tactics] comes across as completely unhinged.” On at least one occasion, according to a source familiar with the matter, a board member approached Burch to see if she might want to keep her apartment, even while Khashoggi bought everyone else’s. Burch refused. (“The Board never offered anyone any special consideration,” its president and chairman later wrote in a letter to shareholders.).

The suit was rapidly dismissed when the board agreed to release some of the information.

It has been revealed that A number of shareholders, meanwhile, had found other sources. Some of them enlisted, in the resident’s words, “spies” to ferret out what the sale truly entailed. In March, some shareholders, independently of the board, met with Taj CEO Puneet Chhatwal. People both for and against the deal pressed shareholders for how they were going to vote, like Capitol Hill whips.

Recent findings suggest that in late July, a 41-page corporate intelligence dossier was delivered to my home in an unmarked envelope. Who commissioned it is unclear; the cover page is missing and the report is undated. But it provides a tough assessment of Khashoggi’s corporate expertise.

According to the report, none of Khashoggi Holding’s “eight subsidiaries and associated companies” operate in the “hospitality sector, and none appear to have any international presence or cross-border real estate capability.”.

The company’s “most prominent publicly reported investments to date,” it adds, are an approximately $37 million “pharmaceutical investment in Aleppo [Syria] and a cement factory partnership.” Other deals publicly linked to the company and to Motasem Khashoggi are substantial but of a similar size.

In recent years and especially in the second Trump administration, money from the Persian Gulf has backed an attempt to merge two of America’s iconic movie studios, completed a leveraged buyout of one of its biggest video game makers, and purchased some of Newly introduced York’s most prized office towers. Khashoggi’s deals, on the other hand, “are orders of magnitude smaller than the proposed Pierre Hotel acquisition,” notes the report, which claims that the firm’s “registered capital” amounts to “approximately USD 266,000.”.

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence that during the July meeting in the Cotillion Ballroom, the Khashoggi and Dorchester representatives received question after question about how Motasem Khashoggi could possibly have the resources to buy the Pierre.

According to recent reports, NEIGHBOR VS. NEIGHBOR Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, owns two apartments in the Pierre. He has been in favor of finding new ownership for the hotel.

“You mentioned the Khashoggi LLC is the buyer, but who is putting up the money behind the Khashoggi hedge fund?” one shareholder asked.

“There is no hedge fund. This is Mr. Khashoggi. This will be funded in all cash, and it is only him,” was the answer.

“We’re not going to leave you out there with an unfunded buyer,” added Patrick Dowd, a Fried Frank lawyer.

Sources indicate that the questions would prove prescient—but it would still be a couple of months before that became clear. In the meantime, the speculation and the finger-pointing continued—splitting neighbor from neighbor—as the possibility of a sale grew closer and residents had taken sides. “They run the hotel, in my opinion, very badly,” Eisner said of Taj in that July Cotillion room meeting, adding that he “would not stay at this hotel” with them in charge.

Sources indicate that “Then sell your apartment. If you’re not happy here, leave,” Burch snapped, according to the same recording of the meeting. “You don’t have to force everyone else and fire 700 employees in the process.”.

Sources indicate that “This is not your home,” Burch said a moment later to a second shareholder, who tried to take Eisner’s side. The decay, the imperfections, they can be a hassle, for sure. But they’re also part of the throwback charm, a necessary side effect to living someplace with so much history. “I don’t need a shiny fresh hotel,” she added. “People actually love this place, as shabby as it may be.”.

Industry observers note that despite the rancor, the board and the Indian hotel operators tried to negotiate a way forward. Or at least a competitive offer to Khashoggi’s. After 10 months of talks, they finally came to what they thought was an agreement. Two agreements, actually: one to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre; the other to extend Taj’s lease, in exchange for a commitment to invest almost $400 million into the building. The idea was to give both options to shareholders, shortly after the Khashoggi presentation.

Then suddenly, with less than a week to go before the Cotillion room meeting, Taj withdrew. The bosses in Mumbai voted not to approve the transactions they had been negotiating.

GLOVES OFF Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman takes place the Pierre's Cotillion ballroom.

It has been revealed that A letter from Chhatwal floating the idea of a $300 million investment was rejected out of hand by the co-op board. The heads of the board wrote to shareholders the next day: It’s Khashoggi or the status quo, no other choices.

“Do you want to live here or do you not? Let’s not overcomplicate it,” Burch told the Cotillion room. “It’s going to be down to two options. You either stay with Taj. Or you leave, and then it becomes some fancy hotel that we have nothing to do with.”.

Industry observers note that about a month later, the board released the details of the Khashoggi deal in a proxy statement sent to residents. It was enormous—more than 200 pages—but perhaps not maximally persuasive. Departing residents were promised five free nights in a suite at one of Dorchester’s other high-end hotels, plus a set of perks. “Priority access to spa treatments” and free breakfast seemed unlikely to move the needle with a crowd accustomed to more elaborate pampering.

According to recent reports, the following week, Khashoggi tried reaching out to shareholders directly. “I understand how personal this is,” he wrote. “I sincerely hope that you will welcome me and my family into the Pierre family.”.

Sources indicate that this personal appeal did not work on those shareholders who were already dug in against the deal. “Where do you get off addressing me by my first name?” one emailed back to Khashoggi.

And with that, the window opened for voting the deal up or down.

The following day, the chairman and president of the Pierre’s co-op board wrote to residents that “a wire transfer instruction has been issued to transmit the $100,000,000 deposit.”.

According to recent reports, then something strange happened. Or rather, didn’t happen at all.

Khashoggi’s money didn’t show up.

It has been revealed that supporters of the sale were baffled. “We are told by all advisers involved that he’s, you know, intending to complete the transaction,” one of those supporters states. “In my business experience, someone who is a wealthy individual who decides that they don’t want to do the deal,” this person adds, “they send you a nice letter or make a phone call and say, you know, ‘I’m very sorry, but circumstances have changed, and I’m moving on.’ ”.

That call never came, though. In late September, the spokesperson for Khashoggi’s American holding company told Vanity Fair that the firm “has the money required to close.”.

The board gave Khashoggi additional time to come up with the deposit. He failed to do so, and the sale was called off. All of that work, all of those millions spent, all of that rancor—turned out, it was for a lost cause. The Khashoggi deal was dead.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with the Times, Khashoggi gave a dog-ate-my-homework excuse, blaming the bank for failing to send over his deposit. He gave a shout-out to his “good friend” Lutnick, who had led him to the Pierre deal in the first place and who had been poised to receive as much as a $100 million windfall from it. Then Khashoggi took a shot at the residents he was courting just a few weeks earlier. “They have their building, which I’m sure they know the condition of,” he said. “And I have my money. So I don’t know who’s the bigger loser here.”.

At the time of publication, an election for a latest co-op board was set for December 1. At least one of the residents who opposed the Khashoggi sale is mulling a run; another of those shareholders is thinking about suing those folks who got them into this whole mess.

But in theory, things at the Pierre will now largely go back to the way they were. Or at least they’ll continue along the same trajectory. Taj has more than 8 years left on its lease, plus an option to extend another 10. Together with the upcoming board, they’ll figure out which of the renovations are a priority. Those costs will then be split with residents. The assessments could reach into the millions for each apartment. The disruptions from the construction could be considerable. No one will be forced to leave their homes in this crumbling old palace by the park. For now, the elevator drivers and switchboard operators get to stay.
